newsitem.title: USA: U.S. condemns Belgrade over election annulment.
newsitem.headline: U.S. condemns Belgrade over election annulment.

text.p: The United States on Monday condemned the authorities in Belgrade for annulling municipal election results which had produced victories for a coalition opposed to Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.

State Department spokesman Glyn Davies told a news conference the annulment was "totally unacceptable" and said: "Such a step undermines the election process and invalidates Serbia's claim to be a state evolving towards democracy."
Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum was sending a personal message to Milosevic to express U.S. rejection of Belgrade's methods, Davies said.
The Yugoslav charge d'affaires in Washington, Nebojsa Vujovic, was also called into the State Department on Monday to hear U.S. criticisms.

Davies said that in a recent meeting in Paris, Secretary of State Warren Christopher had told Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic that "Serbia could not expect to rejoin the international community until it demonstrated commitment to developing into a modern, open and democratic society."

He said: "Because of Serbia's failure to observe democratic principles, the United States has not recognised Belgrade. This recent action confirms our position that Serbia is not committed to meeting Western democratic standards."
After polling eight days ago, Milosevic's Socialists initially conceded they had lost councils in industrial towns across Serbia including the capital Belgrade.
But state-controlled electoral commissions, citing unspecified irregularities, later annulled the results in almost all the districts won by the opposition Zajedno coalition.

Davies said the U.S. reaction at this stage was to "talk about what is going on there and basically shine a spotlight on what we believe the ruling party has been up to" but he said this "would not preclude other actions (that) might be taken."

Washington maintains an embassy in Belgrade but does not formally recognise Serbia and its ally Montenegro as successor to the former Yugoslavia. It also maintains an "outer wall" of sanctions aimed at denying Belgrade access to international financial institutions.

The Washington Post on Monday quoted Serbian opposition leaders as charging that Milosevic had been emboldened to recapture Belgrade by a weak Western reaction to alleged earlier electoral tampering in other major Serbian cities.

It said opposition officials contended that Western powers supported Milosevic because they saw him as the one Yugoslav politician able to enforce implementation of last year's Dayton peace accord in Bosnia.
